Some idea of the situation generally may be had from the following Introductory summary preceding pages of strike news in the San Francisco Call:

Mr. Olney has a bloody mind, but it is questionable whether he himself would have acted with the same level-headed goodness which characterized the conduct of the humblest regular soldier in the ranks at the critical time. Mr. Olney's sympathies are keen, but they are perverted.

U. Added to this is the threat of the advisers of the President to declare martial law and throw the militia of New York into Chicago—measures never resorted to save in time of war. If true the statement is made that Governor Altgeld will be given chance to see what he can do, but behind that statement is the darker threat. When President Cleveland does this, if he does it, the country will be in a state of civil war. Locally, there is no change in the situation. The Southern Pacific is blocked at Oakland, at Sacramento, and at Los Angeles. San Francisco has expressed her sympathy with the strikers, and a company of militia has been sent to open up the coast line at San Jose. The end in matter of the unrest can be seen if it is no nearer than when the strike began."

THE FEDERAL ATTORNEY GENERAL

Attorney General Olney, referring to letter from Governor Altgeld of Illinois to the President, said the soil of Illinois is the soil of the United States. The paramount duty of the President of the United States is to see that the laws of the United States are faithfully executed, and in the discharge of that duty he is not hampered or crippled by consulting any Chief of Police, nor even Governor. Nothing has been done and nothing ordered which the most captious critic can condemn as an invasion of State rights.

The Attorney General further said that the fact that the riotous demonstrations continue only shows that the conduct of the troops not responding with ball and bayonet was of most forbearing character.

REGULAR ARMY INSUFFICIENT.

One result of the big strike has been to show in a startling manner the inadequacy of the United States regular army, which has been reduced to a mere skeleton. rule and the control of their own affairs by
the people of the vicinage." That is the
last paragraph in the home-rule plank of
the democratic platform which Grover
Cleveland achieved the presidency for a
second time. The expression has every ap-
pearance of sincerity and there was an
era of buoyant expectation as long as many
among the District of Columbia democrats
regarded it as perfectly honest announce-
ment by which the chief executive would
surely be governed. But with the nominal
nomination of Charles H. J. Taylor of Kansas as
recorder of deeds for the District of Colum-
bia, fame in the Chicago platform has about
disappeared. Even the most enthusiastic
apologist for the presidential breach of con-
tract cannot find knot-hole in the plank
through which to evade honest and indis-
pense criticism, for the convention declared
in unmistakable language that "we hold
that the officials appointed to administer
the government of any territory, together
with the District of Columbia and Alaska,
should be bona fide residents of the terri-
tory or district in which their duties are
to be performed." In this matter, however,
the President refuses to be bound by the
platform which he pledged himself to sup-
port, and as the people of the District of
Columbia are without that right of appeal to the ballot,
which most other American citizens enjoy,
they can do no more than make vocal pro-
testation against the imposition upon them
of a nonresident. It was fondly imagined
that when the office of recorder of deeds
was legislated into the salaried class that
it would no longer be used as political pap-
er for the sustenance of colored politicians
whose homes were in far away communi-
ties, but the imaginings were vain and the
hopes that blossomed so beautifully but
prematurely, have withered and are now
mingled with the dust. That the President
should have made a local selection, either
white or colored, instead of going to Kan-
sas or anywhere else outside of the District
of Columbia for a nominee, is a conclu-
sion that admits of no debate. The office
is a purely and peculiarly local one. It is
sustained by fees paid exclusively by prop-
erty owners of the District, and the sur-
plus receipts of the office, beyond the sal-
aries and expenses, provide the national
government with revenue which, in all fair
ness, should be, but is not, applied to the
work of local improvement. Mr. Charles
H. J. Taylor cuts but small figure in this
matter. He sought the position, as did at
least one or two residents of the District,
and he received the honor of nomination by
a President who deems himself superior to
his party platform and not amenable to the
rulings of common equity. Mr. Taylor hav-
ing, it is presumed, rendered Mr. Cleveland
important service, had to be paid for the
work he did, but as the Senate failed to
permit Mr. Taylor to represent the United
States as minister to Bolivia, and as the
President did not want to give Mr. Taylor
his personal check, the chief executive
has called upon the property owners
of the helpless District of Columbia to
liquidate his political indebtedness to
the Kansas negro whose name is now be-
fore the Senate for confirmation. It is
reasonable to presume that the Senate Com-
mittee on the District of Columbia will

The story OF the Eccentric Ruskin: Marriage and Divorce.

John Ruskin did a strangely hayward thing when he consented to get married. He did a most erratic and, to the public, a most inexplicable thing when he arranged for his divorce. He had accepted some of the loftiest traditions about womanhood that men sometimes read and talk about, and he looked for his ideal companion. One night he met her in the drawing room of a London friend, who, without his knowing, had brought the young lady to meet the eyes of the great writer.

It was a June night. He was 55, and she looked like a Greek goddess. He was dazzled. She was a tall, graceful girl of in, with face and figure as faultless as one of the statues of old. No one ever expected Ruskin to fall in love, and he did not. She was poor, needed a home and its comforts, and so they were married.

Their wedded life was peaceful, friendly, kindly to the highest degree, but there was no spark of affection to enlighten their existence. She admired the great man she had married and was grateful for the wealth and comfort he showered on her. He worshipped her as he would the marble made lifelike by the sculptor's chisel.

There was nothing human about the life they led as husband and wife, and she was a woman who in her heart like all true women, laughed at the traditions that made her sex love distant worship.

One day Ruskin brought an artist to paint his wife's picture. And the man was Millais and he was a bright, cheeky, handsome fellow, human every inch of him, with a great and absorbing love for the beautiful and a willingness to tell of his love.

He began to paint the portrait of the magnificent woman, and when he had finished he was in love with his friend's wife. Womanlike she saw it, and perhaps she was not full of sorrow and reproach. It was the first tribute of real manly love that he had ever laid at her feet.

And Ruskin, his wide eyes saw the romance that was weaving around those two lives, and his heart realized how little affection he had to lavish on the woman he had made his wife. How he told her the story of his pride in her, and the sacrifice he was to make for her while she lay prone at his feet, is one of the things which only he or she could tell.

It is difficult to obtain a divorce in England, but John Ruskin secured it for her, and one bright morning in the early winter, a month after the divorce was granted, they walked through London's quiet churches and saw them made man and wife.

That was a good many years ago and since then Millais has become rich and famous and is now Sir John, and his wife is Lady Millais. The warmest, sturdiest friend the struggling painter had in his toiling days was the man whose wife he had married and through all the years of Millais' later success and greater honor John Ruskin has been the welcome guest and daily visitor to the man and woman whose lives are so unselfishly crowned with happiness.

Count Posadowsky, Imperial Secretary of the
Treasury, introduced the Financial Reform
bill. He said that certain members of the
House hoped to damage the bill by securing a
postponement of its discussion until after the
single bills connected with the financial re-
forms had been fully dealt with. This was a
tactical move, which, instead of injuring the
imperial Government, would benefit it, for
several of the handbags of the Federal States
had found time and had taken the occasion to
discuss and approve the reforms proposed by
the imperial Government.

ures of the Government's scheme. Among
the opponents of the bill were some who de-
manded that a higher tax than the one pro-
posed be placed on Bourse transactions.
The members, he added, must consider that it
would be imprudent to fell a tree for the pur-
pose of obtaining its fruit.

ment had interfered or was interfering with

the lady and gentleman who break the

The objection to this arrangement is that

queens. The best plan is to have as many

WASHINGTON, June 13.—The brakes were taken off in the senate and more progress was made with the tariff bill than during any previous three weeks of the consideration of the measure. Three schedules—spirits and wines, cotton and flax and jute and hemp manufactures, from paragraph 237 to 217, inclusive, comprising 19 pages—were disposed of.

The entire cotton schedule—10 pages of the bill—was finished in 80 minutes. The Republicans made no opposition to the amendments proposed to this schedule, maintaining that the rates, though reduced, were so arranged as to make the cotton schedule the most "scientific" ever prepared. Bags made of burlap for grain and cotton bagging were placed on the free list.

The collar and cuff paragraph provoked considerable discussion and more or less amusement.

High Tariff on Collars and Cuffs.

Collars and cuffs, in an amendment proposed by Mr. Jones, were made dutiable at 30 cents per dozen pieces and in addition 80 per cent ad valorem; shirts and all other articles of wearing apparel composed wholly or in part of linen, 50 per cent ad valorem.

Mr. Platt of Connecticut took the floor as soon as Mr. Jones' amendments were offered. The rate proposed in this paragraph, he declared, was not only highly protective, but prohibitory. The reduction of the rates in the paragraph was less than 10 per cent, the McKinley rate being as he thought, illustrated the progress of tariff reform—two words that had almost gone out of use in the senate. Before the bill reached the senate this paragraph imposed a tariff reform rate of 30 per cent on collars and cuffs. When the bill was considered in the Democratic senatorial caucus, it was found that 90 per cent constituted the genuine, simon pure tariff reform. But even that rate was not high enough for somebody, and it was changed, he supposed, in consequence of that hard political necessity of which Mr. Vest was so fond of speaking, to 30 cents per dozen pieces and 80 per cent ad valorem. Mr. Platt said he had his own idea of how this high duty came to be imposed on collars and cuffs. There was an old saying, "Scratch a Russian, you will find a Tartar." In this bill, whenever you scratch protective duty, you find Democrat under it. He concluded his remarks with a parody on Bret Harte: For ways that are dark and tricks that are vain, tariff reform is peculiar.

"Is this duty protective or revenue duty?" asked Mr. Aldrich.

"Revenue, of course," replied Mr. Vest.

"It is excessively high," suggested Mr. Aldrich, and rather hard on the poor wearers of collars and cuffs.

"Oh," replied Mr. Vest sarcastically, "I don't think the senator from Rhode Island, who placed 234 per cent on wooden clothing, ought to gag at this duty on collars and cuffs."

"My stomach is not so delicate as yours," retorted Mr. Aldrich.

for the meeting of Congress draws near,
and members and Senators gather into the
capital, the feeling grows stronger that no
further tariff legislation will be accom-
plished by the Fifty-third Congress.
Speaker Crisp, whose judgment on Con-
gressional affairs is unusually good, as his
sources of information are entirely
reliable, evidently has no expec-
tation that the Senate will
pass any of the popgun bills which were
sent to it from the House after the general
tariff bill was adopted toward the close of
the long session. The Speaker knows bet-
ter than most men in public life the power
of the forces arranged against the
bill to put iron ore and coal on
the free list and removing the dif-
ferential duty on refined sugar.
His desire for the enactment of those bills
into law does not deceive him into believ-
ing that the Senators who stood in the
way in the last session will now yield and
let the bills become a law. And he also
knows that even if all the Democratic
Senators should agree to support the pass-
age of the bills, this would not
be sufficient. He understands that
the coal, iron and sugar interests
have even more devoted friends in
the Republican side than elsewhere in the
Senate. These Republicans, in the last
session, did not find it embarrassing to show
their hands very plainly. Some of them
even posed as enemies of the Sugar Trust,
and affected to desire the removal of the
differential duty on refined sugar. But if
there should arise real danger of the re-
moval of this duty, then these Republicans
would appear in their true colors, and find
means of blocking the proposed legislation
by filibustering or otherwise.


As there can be no mistake about the
practical impossibility of getting the pop-
gun bills through the Senate, the feeling
grows that the wisest course for the Dem-
ocrats to take will be not to make the at-
tempt seriously. Of course, it will be im-
possible to prevent individual Senators
from discussing the bills and making clear
in justice to themselves, their desire for
affirmative action on them. But this can
be done without a general re-opening of
the tariff discussion, which might have the
effect of again unsettling business, now
rapidly recovering from the recent discus-
sion.


It is this knowledge that even if the
Democrats of the Senate were united in
favor of the passage of the special tariff
bills, the Republicans would filibuster to
prevent, which makes many Democrats
incline to deprecate a useless reopening of
the agitation.

Of course the carpet had been taken up, so when the wind came round to the north it came straight up at my feet. I hadn't a very good assortment of bedding. Most of our stuff had been sent over to Wenner's warehouse. I had a sheet folded lengthwise, in the form of one of those sleeping bags which explorers use. Then I had an old blanket and for a coverlet one of a pair of fine poufchairs. At 3 o'clock I got up and secured the other poufchair. They were still attached to the poles, but that was rather an advantage than an inconvenience. I put the poles across under my head and thus slightly increased the effective length of the cot.

"A little after I rose again and secured a fur rug. It was a tiger's skin, with the head of the beast on one corner of it. There seemed to be some warmth in that tiger skin, for I secured little sleep almost immediately after spreading it over me. I had left the lamp burning, for I thought it might warm the room a little. Well, sir, as I say, I slept a few minutes just long enough to dream that I was one of the early Christian martyrs in the arena—and I then awoke to find this tiger's head, with its gleaming, glassy eyes staring me in the face. Say, what do you think I did? I yelled so loud that the commotion put the light out. My wife and her sister thought there were burglars in the house. What did they do about it? I don't know, but my opinion is that they crawled into a pile of carpets and rugs in the middle of their room and hid there till morning.

"As for me, the shock of my fright made me shiver; and when I got over being frightened I couldn't stop shivering. How I could be cold with all those things over me I couldn't understand, but it was true. I arose and secured the stair carpet. It went up and down me five times, I remember, but it didn't raise my temperature one degree.

"Then I made the important discovery that it didn't make any difference how much I had over me so long as I had only one layer of canvas under me. And the wind still whistled up through the bare boards, decided to put the tiger's skin over the cot and lie down on it. Then a new inspiration came to me—why not go down and sleep in the kitchen? Good idea, I picked up the cot, the poufchairs, the fur rug and the stair carpet and started for the kitchen. At the head of the back stairs I stepped on the fringe of one of the poufchairs. I endeavored to step off it, but there were five apertures in the fringe, and each one of them had secured one of my toes. Therefore I just calmly fell over forward and slid down stairs with the cot as a toboggan.

"I had fallen down stairs for the kitchen was perhaps a shade warmer than my room, but it was cooling rapidly, and I could not find any warmth there."

World reporter this morning, returned

ade or warning it to prepare for ser-

men during the forenoon.

"Byrnes, Gen. Fitzgerald and other off-
icals, there is not necessarily any sig-
nificance to be attached. We are simply
keeping en rapport with each other."

Lillian Russell, the prima donna, who was married last January to John Chatterton, who sang in her company under the name of Signor Perugini, has written to the public an explanation of why she and her husband are at outs. It is an interesting addition to the written history of popular actress life, and is as follows:

To the Public:—I blame no one but myself. I have been so pressed by my friends for an explanation of my present position that in justice to myself I feel it to be my duty to let the public know some of the reasons which have led me to separate from Signor Perugini.

There seems to be an impression that mere whim or caprice has been the cause of my taking this step. Let me briefly review my career before correcting this impression. I have been before the New York public for fourteen years, always striving to please and to entertain them. I have been ambitious and successful in my art, but, like all other women, have had dreams of happy home and the unselfish congratulations and encouragement of a true husband.

REVIEWS HER MARRIAGES.
Though my lyric successes have been many, my marriages have been signal failures. I married my first husband when I was 18 years old. He was my senior by many years. I was ambitious and grew beyond him rapidly. The incongruity of this union can best be illustrated by the difference in our present professional positions.

My second marriage at the outset promised well. We had everything in common. One object in life was that he should write operas and I should sing them. We spent three years of decided happiness together and a happy future, as we thought, awaited us. The end came abruptly. He went to England on professional engagement, and he was arrested in London for bigamy. When I heard of this and realized that our marriage was illegal, I, as in duty bound, separated from him and secured divorce.

I lived eight years single, working in my profession, consequently giving my best efforts to the public. During my engagement this season at the Casino met Signor Perugini, whom I thought was an ideal man. His whole nature and taste seemed to be so artistic and refined. He appeared to have so much spirituality, and by his grace of manner, his entreaties and the influence of his friends consented to marry him. My consent, however, was reluctantly given and the night before the ceremony was performed I sat and thought gravely over the subject, fearing that I was about to make a mistake.

WAS GROSSLY DECEIVED.
As the sequel showed, I was grossly deceived.

No later than at breakfast on the morning after our marriage my husband began to show disposition to rule me, and to dictate who should be my friends, who should enter my affairs, and what I should do. He threatened at the very outset to discharge my servants, especially my faithful maid, who had been with me for more than seven years. I would have met him more than half way in all these matters had he proven himself husband worthy of the name.

I think when a woman, either a prima donna or otherwise, marries a man whom she can respect as a man, who is the breadwinner and her superior in intelligence, she should never question his methods of business.

But I also think that when the woman is the breadwinner, the superior in both intelligence and disposition, she should also be at least respected, not nagged at and worried as I was for reasons for all she does. A happy home and a devoted husband are more than all the successes that the world can know.

Again I say that I blame no one but myself. I should have known more of the man I accepted as an ideal.

Quarrel after quarrel occurred between us and it was during one of these trying scenes that Signor Perugini admitted to me that he had never loved me, but that he had married me for artistic position purely.

WELDON, N. C., April 3.—(Special).—
The people of this place have had the
pleasure of hearing Virginia's greatest
delineator of the "old-time plantation
negro," Mr. Polk Miller, of Richmond.
He was greeted here last night by a
refined and cultured audience, and his
entertainment throughout was most de-
lightful. His "log-cabin" stories, in-
cidents of the negroes' devotion to the
southern people during the war, o'
possum and coon hunts, his songs, and
pleasing dialect negro stories just car-
ried his audience right along with him,
and kept every one present in con-
tinuous roar of laughter. Mr. Miller is
a born mimic, and there was a charm in
his delivery and songs which were so
far from the conventional flocutionary
efforts that it is really refreshing to
hear him. Every man, woman, and child
in Richmond knows Polk Miller, and he
is brim full and running over with wit
and humor. If he is proud of being a
Virginian, Virginians should certainly be
proud of him. Polk Miller has a great
and brilliant future before him, and there
is a charm in his recitals which cannot
be acquired from book knowledge of the
negro but which only comes from one
who has mingled with the old-time
darby, played with him, and under-
stands his nature from personal contact.
Mr. Miller possesses this knowledge, and
wherever he goes he will delight the peo-
ple with his unique entertainment.

The Republican Executive Committee,
which met here last Saturday, selected
this place to hold their next con-
gressional convention. There are several can-
didates for Congress, and the fight in the
convention promises to be a lively one.

severe. In reference to this state of

people to come to this state is to lay
the facts before them."

of circulars and are growing sceptical
of them.

today will represent the products

Western states will commence coming
to this state and in less than a year
many will arrive from Holland.

Secretary Carlisle was closeted with the President for an hour this afternoon at the Executive Mansion discussing the seigniorage bill. The President is making up his mind on this matter with great deliberation, weighing the facts presented with judicial impartiality. His action in requesting the committee of the New York Chamber of Commerce not to visit him is explained by the statement that he wished to reach a conclusion upon the subject without disturbance from outside persons one way or the other.

Representative Bland of Missouri wishes it be understood that the Committee on Coinage, Weights and Measures, of which he is chairman, has not as a body written from Secretary Carlisle to give any recesses as to their future action in case the seigniorage bill should become a law. The individual members, he says, may have spoken with the Secretary and assured him that if the bill was signed there would be no further silver legislation by the Congress, but if they did this it was in their personal capacity and without any authority from the Committee. Mr. Bland says that he has not written Secretary Carlisle for some time, and only saw the President for a moment, and at that meeting expressed the hope that he would act. But Mr. Bland admits that he has abandoned his crusade for the free coinage of silver. WASHINGTON, D.C., March 6.—The pressure being brought to bear upon President Cleveland in regard to the action he shall take upon the Bland seigniorage bill is not confined to senators and representatives, for he is in receipt of letters and telegrams from all sections of the country upon the subject and contrary to the belief that seems to prevail, a very large majority of these communications urge him to exercise the veto power. Many of the most emphatic of the letters in their urgency for veto are from Baltimore, New Orleans, Richmond, Va., St. Louis, Charleston, Ga., and other Southern cities, and represent boards of trade and leading business men. Similar communications have been received from New York, Chicago, Pittsburg, Allegheny City, Detroit, Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Rochester, N.Y., and Providence, R.I.


The prevailing sentiments contained in these appeals are the expression of an apprehension that should the bill become a law, there would result loss of confidence in the credit of the Government, a fear that the gold would be drained from the Treasury and feeling that the Government would be unable to maintain the parity between gold and silver, thus placing its financial status on the same footing with Mexico, the South American republics, and India.

Resolved, That in the opinion of the representatives of the financial institutions of New York who subscribed to the $4,000,000 five per cent loan and made it a success, the coinage of the silver seigniorage would endanger the financial stability of the Government, and would inflict upon suffering people pernicious and unnecessary legislation, which would be far reaching in its disastrous consequences.


About twenty-five of the leading New York bank presidents and private bankers were present.

The Senator held up a large yellow envelope. "I have plenty of ammunition here. I want the Governor to understand that when I tackle the State administration I shall do it frankly, though in perfect good humor. When I warm his back he must take it like a little man. He must take his punishment. I shall take mine. I am used to it.

I know the farmers are poor. I understood that the Governor promised when elected that he would help the farmers. Are they better off? On the other hand, taxes have been increased. I shall stand side by side with my people in their struggle. I challenge Gov. where I have not done my duty. It is wrong to turn a man out of the Senate because he has done his duty. Echols of Staunton opened fire in favor of the local-option measure, known as the Miller bill. At the opening of session an unusual crowd was present in expectation of the lively scenes of the day before, and when Senator Echols commenced to speak every available space in the chamber was filled with interested listeners, including dozens of ladies. Senator Echols spoke for nearly an hour, and made an able presentation of his side of the case.

Senator Mushbach, at the beginning of Senator Echols' speech, asked permission to say that he would have had something to say in reply to the senator from Gloucester the day before if he were present, but in his absence as he understood on account of sickness he would not reply, as he desired to say what he had to say in his presence, Senator Echols.

Senator Echols said he felt it his duty to his constituents to have something to say in favor of the Miller bill; that he regretted deeply the absence of the senator from Gloucester (Stubbs), who had taken such a prominent part in opposition to it, as he wanted to answer his argument, and disliked to do so in his absence. He had believed that senator Stubbs, having seen the operations of the local-option law, would stand with him, and he was disappointed that his friend had opposed him in this matter. He held that it was never intended that the operation of the local-option law should be so sweeping as to place in the hands of a minority the power to raise these questions which cause quarrels and divisions among friends, among families, and among churches, that the Democratic party had given to the Temperance people good deal more than they had right to claim, and that it was never originally intended in the resolution passed by the Democratic convention that the cities should be included in the law.

He denied that the fight was being made against the temperance people, or that its effect would be to throw the temperance question again into politics, for the reason that the matter had been in politics for the past year through the Prohibition party, and that was the evil that had to be fought.

He referred to the ladies present who had been attracted by the discussion, and assured them that it was not his purpose to break down the temperance cause, but to take from the statute book law which permitted vicious minority in any community to misrepresent the sentiment of the intelligence of the section. He sent to the clerk to be read a copy of petition filed with the court of Staunton for a local-option election, to show that the signers were largely voters who were not taxpayers or representative citizens.

He was making no fight against the local-optionists, and was free to confess that but for the Democrats who were local-optionists he could not have been elected. He held that the law had operated advantageously in the counties but that it was another thing in the city.

He then turned his batteries on Sam Jones, Samuel Small, Bodley, Miller and the Prohibition party in Augusta during the late canvass, and read a circular issued by that party showing that they had used exceedingly doubtful methods in that contest, and that a number of the men who were the most prominent men in affairs were the most active in fighting the Democratic party, and that now the same parties were keeping alive the fires by white and colored clubs in the city of Staunton ready for the May election. He also read extracts from newspapers showing that they were preparing to open a campaign in Norfolk similar to the one last fall in Staunton, and in closing laid great stress on the claim that the matter was already a dangerous factor in politics and a menace to the Democratic party.

The latter half of Senator Echols' speech was clear and forcible and the closing few minutes were highly eloquent.

Ashland, Va. Jan. 8, 1894,

To the General Assembly of the State of Virginia: In the name and by the appointment of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union of the State of Virginia, and in accordance with the expressed directions of that body in convention assembled, I do most earnestly entreat the Legislature not to repeal the local-option law, nor to so amend it as to impair its force or restrict its operation, and I most earnestly pray your honorable body to respect the wishes of the women of Virginia, who though not voters nor desiring to be, are vitally interested in all that affects the welfare of the State, and who without power to help themselves in the cities and towns, as well as the country places, are anxiously watching what you will do. Having found the Democratic party the best and most sure defence in times of trouble, we pray honorable gentlemen of the Legislature to heed our prayer.

When he was buying furniture, grand piano, which in due time arrived at the ranch, and it was on this that Mary was practicing. She did not like the idea of being alone at first, but as she found it impossible to persuade her sister to stay with her she had to make the best of a bad job. She went over the scales carefully every few minutes, taking a look out into the garden to see that her relatives did not get too far away. After finishing one piece she rested a moment, thinking of what she would play next. Suddenly she heard a shutting sound, and, turning around, she saw a large, brown bear standing in the doorway leading to the back part of the house. She was paralyzed with fear, nor scream.

She saw the bear come nearer, and she trembled like a leaf. Oh, how she wished she could faint. But she was a strong girl and couldn't, and the bear kept coming closer, and soon had his paws around her. She gave herself up for lost as she felt the grip, which she knew was deadly, tighten around her and the warm breath of the creature on her face. Looking through the window she could see her relatives lounging around peacefully in the shade of the pines and tried to call them, but her tongue would not move and she closed her eyes, expecting to open them in that happy land of which she had been taught from childhood. But what was this? The bear was not hurting her. He held her gently but firmly in his paws, and was actually licking her face, like a pet dog. She opened her eyes, and the world was the same as usual. She could not tell whether she was frightened or not, but somehow she did not try to scream. She just kept quiet, hoping something would happen to end the agony, which she did not understand. The bear did not hold her more than a second, although it seemed ages to the girl. He did not want to hold her, for he threw her on the door. She was still frightened and expected the beast to jump on her and devour her at his leisure. But instead he turned around, commenced to claw the piano and was evidently delighted with his performance, for he kept time with his feet and looked around approvingly. The people outside heard the clatter but did not pay any attention to it, as they afterward said it was not unusual. Mary will never forgive them for this. The bear began to play furiously, and Mary, seeing a way to escape, took advantage of it and ran away screaming from the room. Her relations first refused to believe her story, but hearing the clatter ran to the window and looked in. Bruin was still at it, and by this time had become so enthusiastic that he was performing a sort of can-can to his own accompaniment. He was in the height of his glory and had found out where the bass keys were, and with these he was particularly delighted. The deep, continuous rumble seemed to afford him the greatest pleasure, and he would execute bars that sounded like the "Cadenza of a Storm at Sea."

He howled and jumped and whirled, and at last concluded his concert by getting on the piano on all fours and executing a jig. At this time Mr. Matthews thought he had better take hand, and he ran into the room with an axe, as that was the only weapon available. The bear did not seem surprised, but got out of the way, and had there been room would have left the house. He was struck several times with the axe, but did not show fright, and the man thought he must have found a tame bear, although he could not imagine where it came from. He then changed his tactics and tried to capture it. As it did not appear dangerous he got hold of it and tried to tie it in the piano cover, but at this the brute's wild nature showed itself, and it got ready to make an attack. Before the man could realize what was coming he heard a deep, angry growl and the next moment was clutched angrily by the monster. The beast could have killed him but it did not want to; it just gave him a good squeeze and threw him violently against the wall. After looking at him a moment the bear went out the door and walked leisurely into the yard. Mrs. Matthews and Mary rushed in and soon had Mr. Matthews back to consciousness. He got up and looked out of the window and saw the bear walking quietly over the hill in the direction of the mountain.

In the senate, on the 1st, Mr. Peters presented petitions from citizens of Pennsylvania for the issue of $50 National treasury notes for the improvements of roads. The tariff bill was taken up, and Mr. Peters continued his speech in opposition to it, yielding, however, to permit Mr. Quay to present the memorial of Philadelphia workingmen in convention in Washington against any change in the tariff laws. In the house, after preliminary business, the house went into committee of the whole upon the diplomatic and consular appropriation bill which, at 3 o'clock, was laid aside and eulogies as the late senator Randall of Louisiana, were pronounced, after which the house adjourned.

In the senate on the 8th, the credentials of Thomas Jordan Jarvis appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Senator Vance of North Carolina, were placed on the table. Mr. Peters' resolution for the appointment of a committee to give hearings to the Coxey army was rejected. Several matters of no general interest were considered, and the tariff bill was taken up. In the house, being District of Columbia day, the session was devoted to matters of local interest.

In the senate on the 9th, after preliminary business, debate on the tariff bill was resumed, Mr. Mills closing the general debate on the democratic side in favor of the measure. He said the bill did not meet his entire approval. He doubted if it met the entire approval of any gentleman on his side of the chamber, but such as it was it should have his cordial support. In the house, the post office appropriation bill for the year ending June 30, 1895, was passed.

In the senate, on the 15th, the income tax on building and loan associations was discussed, and the tariff bill was taken up—the formal reading of the bill being dispensed with. The first line—the defining the date for the measure to go into effect—furnished matter for discussion which occupied the entire session. In the house, the diplomatic and consular bill was discussed.

In the senate on the 16th, Mr. Jarvis, the new senator from North Carolina, appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Senator Vance, was sworn in. Mr. Allen's resolution as to the rights of Coxey and his followers to visit the capitol, to assemble and petition for redress of grievances, was further contested, being vigorously denounced by several speakers. The tariff bill was then taken up, Messrs. Higgins and Dolph addressing the senate. In the house, the diplomatic and consular bill was further considered in committee of the whole, reported to the house and passed.

Entre esos que han hecho esa clase de servicios han figurado muy conspicuamente los hermanos Greens.

Las Vegas hace algún tiempo que estos individuos les habían descubierto la pista de dos de la gavilla perseguida llamados Nestor y Nicanor Gallegos, y solo aguardaban una oportunidad para ir a aprehenderlos. Teniendo ya todo listo, el día 20 salieron de la plaza con rumbo hacia el lugar donde vivían los citados criminales.

article: Few persons suspect that the com mon moth may be utilized as decora- tive artist, but he may be if only one be watchful, patient and acquainted with the creatures habits. The larva of the moth has habit of spinning about itself sort of sac from the ma- terial upon which it feeds. As the worm grows it enlarges this sac by the process of splitting it and inserting new material. Now, if a moth worm that has inclosed itself in red flannel be afterward transferred, sac and all, to white flannel, the growing insect will slit it's red flannel covering and enlarge it with portion of the white flannel. If, then, the worm and the sac be transferred to blue flannel, the creature will in course of time enlarge the sac with blue flannel, and thus clothe itself patriotically in red, white and blue. Entomologist Southwick, of the park department. says that it is no great trouble to put moth worm through this performance.

the mines beyond; past Wall with the
great Pennsylvania railroad round
house and with its breathless engine
pauses at Irwin.


At the mine I was taken first through
the boiler rooms, where there are three
batteries of four boilers each to make
steam for running the machinery inside
and outside the mines. In the engine
room are two enormous wheels with
cable ropes and an indicator to lower
the wagons into the mine. The indica-
tor tells precisely where the descend-
ing wagon is at any moment. The vent-
ilation fan is operated by an enormous
wheel which sucks the air out of the
mine. It is replaced by air from the
shaft and slope. The air required by
law for each man is 500 cubic feet per
minute, for mules 600. The outbuild-

were marvels of cleanliness. At the
entrance of the mine the wagon which
is used to carry the inspectors was
draped in white sail cloth, like a ghost-
ly specter among the somber coal wag-

for me, which was very nice of course,
but it did look like a baby hearse. Here

Mr. Fisher, the outside foreman, placed
me in the care of James A. Thompson,
the mine boss, and with parting look
on all things green and beautiful I
stepped into the elevator and shot
down through the black pit 200 feet in
depth so rapidly that I scarcely had
time to breathe. When we landed
I felt like a lost soul plunged in a gulf of
the deepest despair. Around me over
me, coal—nothing but black, with the
exception of my wagon, which stood out
in bold relief in its white covering, and
made me feel more uncanny than ever.
Grouped about were number of min-

the ordinary miners cap and fasten-
ed into it a tiny lamp which emits
only a wee ray of light, making the
men look simply economical. I had
been supplied with a cap and lantern
before I went down in the mine, so I
suppose my appearance was equally
devilish.


For one mile we went by cable. It
was like a long street, with room for
two wagons to pass. Regular coal
trains are composed of fifty wagons, each
holding about 5000 pounds. The mine
is lined with electric wires, which
enable the miners to tell of trouble at
any time. Seated in the car, I was
obliged to bend considerably, as my
head, in an upright position, would
touch the ceiling of coal. Fancy in all
one sees nothing but coal for miles, with
not a ray of light but that from the
lamps on the miners' caps, which
gleam fitfully through the inky dark-
ness like so many frenzies. At the end
of the cable we were met by the con-

miner and a mule. The mule was
hitched to the car and I inquired if
I might drive. This raised a laugh at
my expense, as the mules have neither
a bridle nor reins, but are guided by
the voice. I was surprised at the
intelligence of these animals, and not-
with the rapidity with which we rolled
through this interminable inky dark-

able. When they leave the mine a
miner puts over one eye a cover, for
they, as they go into the light, become
partially blinded. Then, upon retur-

eye, while the other is becoming ac-

intervals of 100 feet are doors for venti-

enough to hold the boy, who sits not
far from in the morning till 2:30 at night,
and opens and closes the doors as
nine trains pass by. Just a jolly word
from the driver, a "hello" to the
miners, and the boy is alone in
his prison of coal.

rooms numbered like houses, and in
the morning the mine inspectors toy
down to the mines with tiny visits
to every part of the mines. They ran
to report gas when discharging
from the rooms. A fine of at least $50
and a $500 fine. After the mines
have been inspected each miner is
given a thorough check and is told to
carry so-and-so. And there he goes
until his wagon is all
checked and puts his check in a pocket.

great a height as possible and their contents

went down a long depression in the mass,

3. It was a mistake to appoint Commissioners with the powers given to Mr. Blount, without the concurrence of the Senate. As to the question of annexation, it was proper to send a commission, but not as to the question of the governmental authority of the Provisional Government.

4. It was a mistake to suppose that our Minister to the Provisional Government could play the double part of Minister and advocate to the deposed queen.

5. It was a mistake to suppose that there was any authority to subvert the Provisional Government within the lines of peace.

6. It was a mistake to conceal the real purpose of the Executive from the Senate and the people of the nation.

7. It was a mistake to suppose that the final judgment of the nation would not side with the heroic band that had done without bloodshed what our fathers did in the Revolution.

8. It was a mistake to suppose that any international wrong had been committed by our Minister to Hawaii, when the great nations had not remonstrated, but had at once recognized the Provisional Government.

9. It was a mistake to suppose that second-rate craftsmanship at home or in Hawaii was any match for the serene and long-headed wisdom of the Provisional Government.

What is due Hawaii is the immediate recall of our present Minister, a frank apology for our mistakes, the recognition of Republic, if it should be established, and the ultimate annexation of the country, if she wants it, to the State of California. Nothing could have been more helpful to that end than our series of mistakes.

sume business and gather in the reve-

In fact, the managers on most of the

tolerant towards their striking employ-
ees, and have been glad to take them

This action on the part of the directors

which convenes here today, expects
to consist of 5000 delegates.


NEW JERSEY REPUBLICANS.


ELIZABETH, N. J., Oct. 9.—The
Republicans of the Eighth Con-
gressional District meet here to-
day.


THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.


NEW YORK, Oct. 9. The Hebrew
Day Of Atonement begins at sun-
set tonight.


A CHRISTIAN CHURCH CONFERENCE.
BALTIMORE, Oct. 9.—The Associa-
tion of Christian Churches for
Maryland, Delaware and the Dis-
trict of Columbia will hold its
annual convention here from to-
day to Oct. 11.


COBB WILL BE RENOMINATED.


ST. LOUIS, Oct. 9.—Congressman
Seth W. Cobb will today be renom-
inated by the Democrats of the
Twelfth Congressional District.
THE NATIONAL PAINT AND OIL CON-


VENTION.


BOSTON, Oct. 9.—The National
Paint, Oil and Varnish association
meets here today, closing its la-
bors Oct. 11.


THE MASONS OF MISSOURI.


ST. LOUIS, Mo., Oct. 9.—The
Grand Lodge A. F. & A. M. of Mis-
souri, convenes here today.


THEY MAKE IMPLEMENTS.

committee of the recently organized
association of Manufacturers of
Agricultural Implements and Ve-
hicles have arranged to hold the
first annual convention of the as-
sociation in this city today.


FOURNIL WINS FIRST GAME.


NEW YORK, October 9.—Edward
Fournil, champion billiardist of
France, made his debut in this
country at Daly's billiard hall last
night. He played a match game
with DAILY for five hundred points,
fourteen inch balk line, and showed
much skill throughout. The score
was: Fournil, 500; DAILY, 800. Four-
nil's average was 50; Daly's aver-
age 80.


RICH OIL FIND.


WABASH, Ind., October 9.—A tre-
mendous oil strike was made last
night on the Robert Gammel farm
south of Bluffton. When they pen-
etrated the rock the oil came with
a rush and it is estimated that the
well has already produced 800 bar-
rels, all of which was wasted, no
provisions having been made to
care for it. It is good for 1000 bar-
rels every 2 hours.


JAPS CAPTURE CHEZ FOO.


YOKOHAMA, Oct. 9.—It is re-
ported that the Japanese have cap-
tured Chez Foo.


HIT IN THE HEAD.

ton Wilson, manager of the Ohio
Hotel, crushed the skull of Andrew
Fink, a boarder, with cuspidore.
Fink is dying.

Cassidy and J. H. Meyers, two
young men, confessed tonight to
burning eight barns and four resi-
dences in the city during the past
six months. They say they did it
for fun. Both are arrested.

guardian.

was manifest in the flesh. It is interesting
to notice that the temple of Solomon was
plundered by Shishak in the thirty-fourth
year of its existence (2 Kings xxiii, 12), and
II Chron. xii, 2, 4.


20. "Then said the Jews, 'Forty and six
years was this temple in BUILDING and wilt
Thou rear it up in three days?'" Understanding only
natural men, they understood nothing of
spiritual things (Cor. ii., 14).


21. "But He spake of the temple of His
body." See how they perverted His words
and flung them at Him in His agony on the
cross (Mark xiv., 66; John xv., 20). We have
one temple of the Holy Spirit in whom


God and Spirit have come to dwell (Cor. iii. 16, John xiv. 17, 23), we
must not be surprised to find our words
perverted and thrown at us in our trials.
This is a fellowship with Christ which should
make us greatly rejoice.


20. "When, therefore, He was risen from
the dead, His disciples remembered that He
had said this unto them, and they believed
the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had
said." The WHOLE of this gospel was written
with the special object of proving that Jesus
is the Son of God (chapter xx., 31), and it
was by the resurrection that He was with
power declared to be the Son of God (Rom.
i., 4); this may account for its early mention
and emphasis in this gospel. It is only when
we are risen from the dead or translated to
meet our Lord that it shall fully appear that
we are sons of God (I John iii., 2).

the passover in the feast day, many believed
in His name when they saw the miracles
which He did." This is the great gospel of
believing. It is found more times in this
gospel than in the other three and in the
Acts all put together. The true meaning of
believing is seen in chapter ii, to be this,
receiving of Him as our own Saviour. To
believe about Him is of no avail unless we
become fully identified with Him in His
death and resurrection and with Him at
God's right hand and with Him in present
service here.

unto them, because He knew all men." The
word "commit" is the same word which is
translated "believe" in the preceding verse.
The V. has it "trust." Jesus, knowing
all men, knew whom He could trust or be-
lieve, and was never deceived in any. He
treated them upon their profession. If they
meant what they said, He gave them every
possible opportunity and help to prove them
selves sincere, but He thoroughly knew them
all the time.


25. "And needed not that any should tes-
tify of man, for He knew what was in man."
He, being God, could read peoples' thoughts.
He is the Lord who searches heart and rein
(Jer. xvii, 10; Rev. ii., 23). For interesting
instances of His mind reading see Luke v.
9, vi, 8; Matt. xi., 11; Mark xiv, 71, and re-
member Mark xii, 25, "For know the thing
that cometh into your mind, every one of
them." I have often been glad that He
knew all that was in me before He ever let
me know that He loved me, for He had
known all my possibilities for evil before I
started with Him; He might have been tempted
to give me up many a time. But whom He
loves He loves to the end (John xiii., 1).

tee censuring Minister Stevens, and Mr.
Outhwaite (Ohio) addressed the House.
As a preface to his remarks he said he
should have nothing to say against Presi-
dent Harrison or Secretary of State Fos-
ter and he had no doubt that Mr. Harri-
son made a good President from
Republican point of view.

But he did endorse the action of the
present President, and also the policy
which declared that the Islands should
not be allowed to fall into hands of
any foreign Government.

Mr. Culbertson (Dem., Tex.) defended
the resolution in a legal argument.

Mr. Storer (Rep., Ohio) made a strong
legal argument against the legality of
the appointment of Mr. Blount as commis-
sioner to Hawaii while the Senate was
in session.

Mr. Everett (Dem., Mass.) defended the
course pursued by Mr. Cleveland. He
said that he had decided the case on
its merits as a judge, as a justice, and
as a man, but when he found he could
not restore the Queen without force, he
referred the whole matter to Congress,
for he was not a man to wade through
slaughter to a throne and shut the gates
of mercy on mankind.

Mr. Loud Tells what He Saw.

Mr. Loud (Rep., Cal.) who was the next
speaker, prefaced his remarks with the
statement that last spring he had visited
the Hawaiian Islands and had remained
there two months, so that he spoke as
one who had personal information on the
subject. As a result of an interruption
he said he had not gone to Hawaii to spy
on Blount, but to his interests, and he
thought it was a mistake to trust in
explicitly to one man instead of commis-
sion, for no one man was free from the
taint of prejudice.

In the course of his remarks he said:
"Blount went to Hawaii to attain a
certain object; went there untrammeled
by object for the purpose of calmly look-
ing at both sides of the question, that I
might the better perform my duties mere-
ly as a legislator upon a subject which all
knew must come before us for review.
So there we parted company—he to re-
sume his star-chamber investigation,
and I to go upon the highways and into the
byways, in the broad light of day, seeking
light."

Mr. Loud reviewed the testimony of the
Blount report by the light of his own
investigations, and asserted that on that
testimony Blount's conclusions were dis-
proved. He said if Stevens had been
guilty of the acts charged it was the duty
of the Executive "to bring him home in
chains" and the laws of his country
would have punished him.

Mr. Loud's conclusions as to the manner in which the provisional government
was organized, after a full examination
of the testimony and personal inves-
tigation during April and May at Hon-
olulu, Mr. Loud stated to be that gov-
ernment of the people and by the peo-
ple of intelligence and decency had at
last been formed in Hawaii, and without
the assistance in the slightest degree of
the minister or the naval forces then
there.

Mr. Turner (Dem., Ga.) defended Mr.
Blount from the charges which had been
made against him, and attacked the pro-
visional Government. He was opposed to
the policy of territorial extension and
drew "a lesson from the fact that when
Rome entered on a similar policy her
power began to decline."

Mr. Slichter Bolts His Party.

Mr. Slichter (Dem., N.Y.) created a
sensation by attacking the party's
policy. He was the first Democrat who
had not upheld the resolution of the
Foreign Affairs Committee. He held that
one administration should not constitute
itself a court of appeal or review on a
deciding administration. (Loud applause)

The question of provision was "res adjudicata," and no one should propose that that question
should be reviewed. He noted a
number of instances in which it was
shown that this country had pursued a
policy of annexation. President Fillmore
had negotiated a protectorate over the
isthmus of Panama, and that had
stood for many years. The same thing
had done in Nicaragua, when it became
probable that the route from the Pacific
to the Atlantic would be built there, thus
giving the United States control there.
In referring to the pending resolution
of the foreign committee, he said he
could not endorse it, and he would not
vote for it. (Republican applause)
He closed his remarks with the pro-
position that no matter what might be the
action of the House to-day, it could not
change the decree of destiny that sooner
or later the Hawaiian Islands would
become a part of the United States.
(Loud applause on the Republican side)
Mr. De Forest (Dem., Conn.) defended
the foreign affairs resolution, while Mr.
Hepburn (Rep., Iowa) spoke in opposi-
tion to it.

Mr. Hooker (Dem., Miss.) was the last
speaker, and in a long speech he at-
tended the resolution of the Foreign Af-
fairs Committee.

At 8:30 the previous question was or-
dered and a vote was first taken on Mr.
Loud's amendment approving the recog-
nition of the provisional government
of the Hawaiian and Cleveland adminis-
trations, and declaring it was a mistake.
Mr. Loud's amendment was defeated on
a standing vote of 111 to 155, and on a roll-
call of 90 to 105.
A vote was then had on Mr. Hitt's
substitute. This declares the sense of this
House that the President's demand on the
provisional government to surrender and
his attempt to erect a monarchy in its
stead was an unwarranted interven-
tion in the affairs of a friendly recognized
government, contrary to the law of na-
tions, the policy and traditions of this
Republic, and the spirit of the Consti-
tution. Also, that the provisional So-
vereignty, having been recognized, the high
international interests require that it be
allowed to pursue its own line of policy, and foreign
intervention will be regarded as an un-
friendly act to the United States.

This substitute was lost—yeas, 105; nays,
155.

Mr. Reed Leads a Filibuster.

Mr. Reed moved to recommit, and this
was lost—yeas, 81; nays, 117. Mr. Gun-
ning (Dem., N.Y.) voting with the Re-
publicans, Mr. Reed demanded the yeas
and nays, and the motion was again de-
feated—yeas, 60; nays, 137.

All were strictly party votes, except two.

the groundnut as probable or actual
substitute for cocoa-or roasted, ground,
and prepared in the same way as choco-
late. He mentioned that in Spain the
earth chesnut was even then being
consumed as substitute for coffee.
The quality of peanuts, however, varies
much more than might be supposed.
The poorest are found on the Madras
coast and the best in the region of the
Senegal, in West Africa, and it is, ar.
parently, only since they began to de-
velop an interest in Africa that the
Germans have discovered the food value
of this humble product.


In 1898 upward of 10000 tons of pea
nuts were imported into Germany, of
which $500 tons came from West
Africa, $500 tons from East Africa. and
the rest from the East Indies. For the
manipulation of the peanut there arc
now twenty-seven factories constantly
employed at Hamburg, Mannheim,
Heilbronn and elsewhere.


The imports from West Africc are in
the shell, which, while making them
more bulky and adding to the freight,
has compensating advantages. For in
stance, the nut is apt to be crushed or
injured when shipped without the
husk, and also to become strong, if not
rancid, in flavor by exposure.


The husks make up about 25 per cent
of the weight of shipment, but are
not all loss, even when their protective
functions are over, for in Germany they
are used in rough papermaking, and
also, when ground up, as food for cat
tie. From West Africa and India the
nuts are usually imported without the
shells-the reason doubtless being to
secure cheaper freight.-All the Year
Round

us—and "for about thirty minutes
work.")


The Judge wrote us for particulars,
having been unable to identify the
case, and later sent us the bill of fees
as of record.


On inquiry by the lady, he had hast-
ily footed up the fees and told her the
amount was $3.50. Later when he
had leisure, he recast the column of
figures and that in his first footing he
had made an error of six dollars,
having mistaken a figure one for a
seven) thus reducing the amount of
fees about one-third, from $3.50 to
$3.50, which, as per the fee-bill sent
us, is less than the legal rate.


This "much ado about nothing" has
therefore, all been the result of an
error, and although inflicting little
punishment on our Probate Judge to
the end may produce other than ill
effects. We have learned, for instance
that Judge Naugle doesn't "gobble
every dollar in sight," as we have
heard some of his left-handed friends
charge; that he is courteous even in
the face of ASSAULT; that he is willing
to make wrong right and assume the
fault of his mistakes, and that he is
doing his level best to handle the affairs
of his office with credit to himself and
honor to the county. And we hope
he may be able to carry his task
through successfully to the end.

And then he told Liza that she must go and change her dress and be photographed now in the way he wished. She came down again, looking so much prettier in her working clothes. Now he was in his element. He arranged Liza and Hans on the sledge of timber which had then dried up, and made a picturesque group of them all, Hans and Liza sitting side by side on the timber, the horses standing there so patiently after their long journey through the forests, the driver leaning against his sledge smoking his long china pipe.

"That will be something like a picture," he said to Bernardine when the performance was over. "Now I am going for about a miles walk. Will you come with me and see what I am going to photograph, or will you rest here till I come back?"

She chose the latter, and during his absence was shown the treasures and possessions of the Swiss peasant's home.

She was taken to see the cows in the stalls and had lectures given her on the respective merits of Schneewitchen, a white cow, Kartoffelkuchen, a dark brown one, and Roselin, the beauty of them all. Then she looked at the spinning wheel and watched the old hausfrau turn the treadle. And so the time passed, Bernardine making good friends of them all.

Catharina had returned to her knitting and began working, and as before not noticing any one. But Bernardine sat by her side, playing with the cat, and after time Catharina looked up at Bernardine's little thin face, and after some hesitation stroked it gently with her hand.

"Fraulein is not strong," she said tenderly. "If Fraulein lived here, I should take care of her."

That was a remnant of Catharina's past. She had always loved everything that was ailing and weakly.

Her hand rested on Bernardine's hand. Bernardine pressed it in kindly sympathy, thinking the while of the girl's past happiness and present bereavement.

"Liza is betrothed," she said as though to herself. "They don't tell me, but I know. I was betrothed once."

She went on knitting. And that was all she said of herself.

Then, after a pause, she said, "Fraulein is betrothed?"

Bernardine smiled and shook her head, and Catharina made no further inquiries. But she looked up from her work from time to time and seemed pleased that Bernardine still staid with her. At last the old mother came to say that the coffee was ready, and Bernardine followed her into the parlor.

She watched Bernardine drinking the coffee and finally poured herself out a cup too.

"This is the first time Herr Allitsen has ever brought a friend," she said. "He has always been alone. Fraulein is betrothed to Herr Allitsen—is that so? Well, I am glad. He is so good and so kind."

Bernardine stopped drinking her coffee.

There are more than the average number of "To Let" signs about town this year and they are not displayed chiefly in vacant or newly completed houses, shops, or stores, but where active business is being transacted, or where the resident tenants appear to have no desire to move. Not for many years, if ever before, have there been, months in advance of May, so many "To Let" signs on tenants' premises in New York. TESTIMONY Before the

House Naval Committee.

Washington, May 25.—The congressional investigation into frauds and irregularities in naval armor plate began to-day with open doors. Representative Dunphy stated that his information came from documents sent to the departments from official papers and from the newspapers. Mr. Dunphy's statement detailed the early discovery of the irregularities and the investigation made by the navy department which led to the finding of the Carnegie company. Mr. Dunphy said armor plates had been tested at the Indian Head proving grounds, and had been found defective. It had then been treated so as to overcome the defects.

"Was this treatment in secret?" asked Chairman Cummings.

Mr. Dunphy answered in the affirmative. He said that one plate was picked out as a sample of a large number of plates, amounting to 345 tons. When this secret retreatment had been made it served to pass the sample plate, and that in turn passed the entire 345 tons of armor.

Mr. Dunphy then spoke of blow holes in the armor of the monitor Terror. Experts had gone to the navy yard and successfully had located two blow holes which had been filled up to deceive the government. Similar blow holes existed in the armor of many other ships, but it was impossible for the experts to locate the defects, as the ships were abroad at their stations. Recent charges covered not only armor plates but the bolts and screws securing the plates. In conclusion Mr. Dunphy said:

My information is that the defective plates will be found on the Oregon, the Machias, the Castine, the Monadnock, the Cincinnati, the Terror, the New York and the Monterey, and that the exact position of the plates on each of these vessels can be located. He added that the defective plates located by the government experts had been estimated to be worth $100,000 to $1,000,000.

Capt. Sampson, chief of the ordnance bureau, navy department, to-day resumed his statement before the house committee investigating the armor plate frauds. He took up the second charges made against the Carnegie company which have been in part investigated by the navy department. Capt. Sampson detailed the charges made by Mr. Wallace, a Pittsburgh lawyer, representing a half-dozen employees of the Carnegie works. Secretary Herbert, Capt. Sampson said, had designated a board with witnesses at hand. They had gone to Homestead and had found the charges and the evidence substantially similar to that at the first investigation. The final report of the board was not yet completed, but in substance it would disclose little that was new.

Mr. Sill, one of the informers in the first investigation, had the most comprehensive knowledge of the defects. None of the witnesses at the second hearing had material information to add to that already given by Mr. Sill. The only thing in the bill of additional information was given by Mr. Kountz and Mr. Bug. The latter testified to a practice in the works of so fixing specimens as to give false records of the tests. He testified that the practice continued until Jan. 1 last. Another employee testified that the practice had always existed. Other workmen swore that the practice had continued until orders were given to discontinue it.

Elias Davis, of New Castle township, candidate for the Republican nomination for Sheriff, is so well known to the voters of Schuylkill county, that it seems superfluous at this time to relate either his personal or political history. During the past eight years he has been almost constantly in public life, the intervals between the terms of his public service being devoted to commercial pursuits, which have brought him in contact with the whole people of the county and enabled him to cultivate acquaintance more extended, perhaps, than any other candidate on either ticket enjoys.

Mr. Davis was born in VAUDEVILLE, Schuylkill county, in November, 1866, and is therefore 28 years old. He began work at the breaker as a slate picker in 1874, when he was but eight years old, and continued to work in and around the mines until he was elected to the Legislature in 1884. In his boyhood he attended school in the winter months and acquired a very fair common school education, and when he grew to manhood his knowledge, ambition and energy made him a leader among the workingmen of his district. He has been prominently identified with every movement inaugurated for the amelioration of the condition of labor, and has always been regarded as a safe, wise and conservative counsellor on matters of this kind.

Mr. Davis entered politics in 1886 as the representative of the workingmen of this district and was supported by them regardless of party. He received the Republican nomination for Assemblyman and was elected by a handsome majority in 1888 and served with credit to himself and decided advantage to his constituents and the workingmen of the mining districts of the state.

Mr. Davis is one of the very few men who have been elected to the Legislature as a representative of workingmen, and who have accomplished anything of advantage to their constituents. His knowledge of mines and mining secured him a position on the Mines and Mining Committee of the House during his first term of service and while in that position he did some good work in the interest of the people he represented.

Mr. Davis is entitled to the full credit of having framed, introduced and passed the semi-monthly pay bill, under which the miners of the anthracite coal region now receive their wages every two weeks. The credit of that achievement he does not share with anybody. It was his own creation, and it was his own individual effort that secured its passage. He has secured the passage of several other acts of less importance but all advantageous to the workingmen of the state, which want of space here forbids us to enumerate. Mr. Davis is a representative of the workingmen of the county in the fullest and most comprehensive sense of the term. He has rendered faithful and valuable services in their behalf and is full of politics. We look for his nomination on Monday next on the first ballot, and his election in November by sweeping majority.

passage of few unimportant bills by
unanimous consent, nothing was done
by the house today. Mr. Boutelle of-
fered resolution congratulating and
recognizing the Hawaiian republic, but
on point of order it was referred to the
committee on foreign affairs.


Two hours were spent in an attempt
to secure the adoption of special order
for the consideration of Mr. McRae's
bill to protect public forest reserva-
tions, but the Republicans by absenting
themselves succeeded in forcing an ad-
journment.


Under the act of March 5, 1898, the
president reserved public timber lands
from sale and disposal, and set them
aside for forestry purposes. The total
number of acres reserved aggregated
11,564,500 acres, and included lands in
Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado,
New Mexico, Oregon, Washington and
Wyoming.


The bill for which consideration was
sought today empowered the secretary
of the interior to sell under restrictions
lands of commercial value on these res-
ervations, to regulate the occupancy of
the same and to protect the same
against fire and depreciation. The
house adjourned at 4:45.

dynamite seemed to affect the usual
source Of moisture and conditions
grew from scarcity of water to none
whatever in many wells, springs, creeks
and rivers. While many crops half
grown perished on the face OF the
earth, potatoes in some cases were
reported as shriveled and partially
baked under ground. Under these
alarming conditions, in view of the
coming winter, many families disposed
as best they could of their loose pro-
perty absolutely giving live stock
away to save it from perishing in many
cases) and came to their eastern
homes or sections more favored with
rain in the hope of finding enough to
sustain life for themselves and little
ones. 1t is possible that some may
return to their deserted western homes
when seasons are more favorable,
but 1t is quite probable that many
never will. The severity Of the drought
this far east indicates what may easily
befall this more favored section any
season. Should it come, with all the
severity that it fell upon Nebraska
and other western States this season,
the suffering would be even greater
because Of the denser population
which is largely reliant upon what
home producers get from mother
earth. And as to bombarding the
heavens for rain, whether science
suggest it or not, there is nothining in
it, we verify believe but to further
offend the only Power that is able to
send us rain or to with hold 1t until
we perish from the face of the earth.
Let us respect this Power.

Teddy Dolson, the bicycle rider on
Friday night had an experience compared
with Mike Finn Shautel's famous ride
pales into insignificance. Instead of the
horse with which Finn was equipped, Teddy
had a bicycle. In the place of the
witches that pursued and plagued and almost crazed the Scotsman, the Cheyenne
man was followed by hungry coyotes.
Finn, too, had taken a generous ration
of usquebaugh, while Dolson's only
preliminary refreshment was a hearty sup-
per.


Friday evening, according to his habit,
Dolson started out for a bicycle ride. He
had intended to go ten miles south,
then return, but being unacquainted with
the country, lost his way, and in trying
to regain his bearings lost himself
entirely. He wheeled in the direction
that Cheyenne seemed to him to be, at
about 5 o'clock at Wheel, twenty miles from the city.


There he was directed how to get back
to town and started on his trail. On
and on he rode, but in no fixed direction,
for in the darkness he had promptly lost
track. As he wheeled along in the
gloomy night over the untracked prairie,
wishing for nothing on earth so much as a comfortable bed, he became suddenly
aware of the fact that he was being close-
followed.


Behind him was a pack of yelping, howl-
ing coyotes, that were close upon him
before being noticed. Their intention was
so evident that his waning energies were
awakened with a thrill. He bolted over
his wheel and pushed it as fast as he
could over hill and valley, and was
closely followed by the coyotes.


To add to his misfortunes, he broke
a pedal in attempting too great strides, and
was on the point of giving in at last
and letting the hungry coyotes do their
worst when he spied a dark shack a
short distance away. To this he fastened
and, abandoning his bicycle, quickly
climbed up on the roof, as high as he
could get from the ground. Even here the coyotes
followed him, but a congenial vantage and
a place of refuge was found on the top of
the chimney.


All night he remained there; at times
driving away his pursuers with fragments
of brick, which caused their retreat to a
short distance, whence, after a series of
lugubrious howls, they would return to
the attack. At daylight they departed with
a parting salute of angry howls, and Dol-
son climbed down and mounted his bicy-
cle, soon reaching Pierce station, on the
Denver Pacific, thirty-eight miles from
Cheyenne.


He was unable to get breakfast until he
reached Cary, and arrived here at 12 o'clock
the next morning. The hardest feature of
the whole night's experience to bear, he
said, was the fact that he had two cigars in
his pocket, but no match to light
them. He was very badly used up by
the night's experience.—From the Cheyenne
Wyoming Leader

The words fitted themselves to the ringing of the horses' hoofs. She knew Mr. Tracy; she had seen him in Virginia City. He was a noted gambler, very gentlemanly in appearance.

The sun was rising as she approached the Golden Eagle Halfway House. She thought she would stop there and inquire if he had gone by. Dismounting from her foaming horse she timidly entered. "Is Mr. Tracy here?" she inquired of the bartender.

The man eyed her curiously. She was covered with dust and her face was pale and haggard.

"Jack Tracy," he said, civilly enough. "Why yes; he's playing with some gents in the other room. Want to see him? I guess they're about through."

She was trembling in every limb. Now that she had found him she did not know what to say, but when he came to her in the musty parlor she told him how she had ridden all night to find him and how her lover was ruined.

"Oh, Mr. Tracy," she concluded, "give me the money! He has been so good to me and I love him! It is all for me that he has spent his money and now I am—"

Jack Tracy looked down into her pleading eyes. "Little one," he said, gravely, "I will give you the money, will you kiss me?"

"Yes, oh, yes," she answered.

He smiled at her eagerness. "It is all for his sake," he said, half sadly. "But never mind." He held her in his arms a moment then pressed the gold into her hand. "Two hundred dollars for a kiss," he said, lightly. "You had better ride my horse back, sweetheart."

He made her drink a glass of wine, helped her to mount his horse, then went inside, saying to himself, "Jack Tracy, you're a fool." As for Favorita, she turned her horse's head towards Yuma with a light heart, the gold hidden safe in her bosom.

A woman of the town, known as Gertie, took morphine with suicidal intent last evening but was pumped out by Dr. Guinan in time to prevent funeral. The morphine route out of Carson is not regarded as infallible any more.

There is proposition on foot to build WOODEN mill in Reno, says the Reno Journal. A committee has been appointed to canvas public sentiment in regard to the matter and to call public meeting if thought desirable Monday evening. It is hoped that the plan will materialize. What Reno needs is manufacturing to make her people prosperous.

Miss Hadley French who has been attending the University for the past two years, yesterday returned to her home in Carson. Circumstances over which she has no control will necessitate her severing her connection with that institution possibly permanently. She leaves large circle of friends who regret her departure.

The Arizona blacksmith, I. J. Partridge, who created such sensation in Los Angeles curtly days ago by producing the sum of $13,800 while undergoing examination for insanity, is declared to be only in need of rest and proper sustenance. For the past fifteen years he has been hard working man, boarding every cent he earned and almost starving himself, which unbalanced his mind.
